speakeroldname: Mr. Ambrose Hubert Peddle (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: MR. PEDDLE-TWENTY-SECOND ANNIVERSARY OF NEWFOUNDLAND'S ENTRY INTO CONFEDERATION WITH CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. My question of privilege concerns an incident which took place at one minute before midnight on March 31, 1949, 22 years ago, a number of some significance to the Prime Minister.
It was on this date, March 31, 1949, at one minute before the witching hour of midnight that nocturnal nuptials, or one might say a midnight marriage, took place between Newfoundland and Canada. The Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, affectionately known as Uncle Louis, bore the ring, and Joey Smallwood, affectionately and otherwise known as Joey Smallwood, the shotgun.
For hon. members who are curious about the strange, eerie hour, here is the official explanation. There was a conflict of interest between one faction which wanted the event to coincide with the very beginning of the new fiscal year and the other faction which at any cost wanted to avoid All Fool's Day. Thus this mysterious but very delicate balance was struck.
Newfoundland was a good deal older than Canada, but despite the age differential 52.34 per cent-here is a significant number again-of Newfoundlanders felt the marriage could be successful while 47.66 per cent felt the marriage could never work. Most of us who supported Confederation felt sure it would survive at least 22 years, but had we known the only living father thereof would survive that long as premier the marriage might never have been solemnized. Anyway, we can take solace in the fact that he has been the best premier Newfoundland has had since Confederation.
Seriously Mr. Speaker-I see you are clutching the edge of your chair so I shall end soon-on this the twenty-second anniversary of Confederation, while I cannot speak nor would I presume to speak for our estranged brother, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson), who wept bitterly when the banns were announced 22 years ago, I am sure that, generally speaking, we
Newfoundlanders on this side of the House supported Confederation and, whether we did or not, we are proud to say today "We are Canadians".

MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 LABOUR RELATIONS EFFECT OF RAIL TRAFFIC DISRUPTION ON GRAIN MOVEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, under Standing Order 26 I ask leave to move a motion for the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the disruption of rail traffic and its present consequences, particularly on the movement of grain to meet Canada's export commitments. This emergency calls for discussion of measures that can be taken immediately to get prairie grain aboard ship at Vancouver to meet these commitments, for discussion of action to ensure that isolated communities get supplies, for discussion of the appointment of an independent conciliator to bring the railways and unions to settlement as quickly as possible in the national interest, and discussion of the appointment of a task force or other body to recommend longterm plans for the settlement of such disputes on the basis of public convenience and necessity. If this proposal is acceptable to you, Mr. Speaker, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. Thomas), that this House do adjourn for this purpose.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 LABOUR RELATIONS EFFECT OF RAIL TRAFFIC DISRUPTION ON GRAIN MOVEMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member for Athabasca has given the Chair due notice of his intention to move the proposed motion under the terms of Standing Order 26. In dealing with the matter stated, I think I owe it to the Chair, to the hon. member and to the House to refer once again to the form of the motion proposed by the hon. member.
The House well knows that Standing Order 26 requires that notice should be given to the Chair accompanied by a statement of the matter to be considered, and that the statement made by the hon. member in the House under the terms of Standing Order 26 should not go beyond the notice which has been given to the Chair, should be limited entirely to a statement of the matter itself, should not include enumeration of circumstances, and should not include any argument. I suggest' respectfully to the hon.
Motions jor Papers
member that again the form is perhaps somewhat defective, and I would hope hon. members would try to bear this in mind. Of course, in such an important matter I would not think I should rule on it entirely from the procedural aspect. I think the situation is so important that it does require substantive and substantial consideration by the Chair.
As the hon. member for Athabasca knows, a similar motion was proposed in the House just the day before yesterday by the hon. member for Moose Jaw. At that time I suggested to the House that the Chair should not overlook the condition and it is a very important one, that there can be only one discussion about a question during the same session under the terms of Standing Order 26. So there is a considerable responsibility on the part of hon. members and on the part of the Chair, when a serious condition is developing, to ensure that the debate, if one is permitted under Standing Order 26, should come at the appropriate time. I am not convinced that the situation has changed so much since Monday that a debate should be allowed today. I am very anxious to follow the matter as closely as possible along with hon. members and perhaps in consultation with them, so that if the point should be reached where it appears that it would be advantageous to the House, to Parliament and to the country that an emergency debate should take place, a motion under Standing Order 26, would be granted.

speechtext:
Sir, as I look over these clauses I can only conclude that the Liberal members will be choosing as their song "Roll Out The Barrel". Over the years there has never been a case that has equalled these particular clauses in respect of the interest they provide for members of the Liberal party. Indeed that is understandable, because if this bill becomes the law of the land and the

March 31, 1971

increases take place in the field of ministries of state and parliamentary secretaries, since these appointments are for a two-year period 110 of 155 Liberal members will have held a position of some kind from cabinet minister to minister of state to parliamentary secretary. In other words, this Parliament will be dominated by those who hold positions within the pay of the country, over and above their indemnity as members. That can only be destructive of the basic principle of the independence of Parliament.
I am very much concerned about this legislation. It is in the Prime Minister's name, but for some reason the Prime Minister does not see fit to be present when discussions are taking place in respect of a matter which is dangerous to the whole concept of parliamentary sovereignty. I shall begin, Sir, by referring to the revelation made the other evening by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister when, in answer to a matter raised by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants, he said that "the bill gives flexibility and raises a dilemma concerning how much debate we can stand". I have left out some of the additional words. That is the attitude of this government; Parliament is to be subject to flexibility which has become a synonym for political patronage. This action is being taken in order to keep in line back bench members in supporting the government. There can be no other reason for such anxiety to get this legislation through, which is described as being urgent. Parliament is being bamboozled with the introduction of this type of legislation. We want action taken in respect of pollution, but in order to secure that action, in my opinion Parliament is asked to itself to engage in pollution.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
In other words, Parliament is being asked to provide jobs for hungry members who are desirous of holding some title or place, not forgetting that various amounts up to $15,000, in the case of ministers of state, will be available. There is every opportunity to appoint ministers without portfolio, but to positions only paying $10,000, and therefore the government decided it would set up another group known as ministers of state.
Then, so far as parliamentary secretaries are concerned, they believe it will not be long before the amount payable to them may be expected to be increased. Last evening the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte condemned this joining together of legislation that Parliament wants with mercenary provisions like this which must be recognized as being a raid on the public treasury for the benefit of a majority. Why is this course taken? Why is Parliament to be treated in this way? Everything is in this particular bill but the kitchen sink!
But there are two provisions in the bill, in this clause and the following one, that possess an unusual attraction for those who up to the present have not had that preferment that they had hoped to have. When I look at this bill, I can understand full well how the Prime Minister and some of his ministers must have laughed with cynicism when it was before the cabinet-"Watch us; we can get away with it." At a time when there are hundreds of thousands of people out of employment because
Government Organization Act, 1970 of the actions of this government, for members of Parliament to join in increasing their opportunities for service at higher rates of pay is something that cannot be justified.
There are so many hon. members opposite just waiting in the wings. I watch them, Mr. Chairman. But the hon. member for East York is not in their number. He is in the dog house, and the numbers occupying that position are increasing with the passing days. Others look with hope and expectation, and I am just wondering whether or not the provisions of Standing Order 11 may have some application. That Standing Order reads:
No member is entitled to vote upon any question in which he has a direct pecuniary interest, and the vote of any member so interested will be disallowed.
You are fortunate, Mr. Chairman, that you do not have to determine this. If perchance that rule is in effect, this bill will be defeated. You can be absolutely sure of that, because as I look over and watch these hopefuls I conclude that even with the increase in positions which this will provide, where 70 per cent of the government members will hold positions of this kind, unless that 70 per cent were voting for it this bill would not pass the House.
I ask myself why is Parliament being treated in this way? I am disquieted by this type of legislation. It is dangerous to the maintenance of Parliament itself when a government has a majoriy and, being afraid to introduce these two clauses, with provision for ministers of state and an increase in parliamentary secretaries by way of separate amendments to existing legislation, it throws them into a hopper and says Parliament must accept all the bill whether we agree with these provisions or not.
This bill has all the hallmarks of the dictatorship of the majority. I am not going to use the type of language which is now passable in Parliament-I am not used to using words of that type. However, this bill is a fraud and a political swindle on the institution of Parliament, and it cannot be justified in any way. It is designed to place private members supporting the government in a position where they dare not speak out, where they dare not have their own opinions, as four or five of them have had, including the hon. member for East York to whom I have alluded. They dare not speak out because in doing so they will commit suicide. The sword of Damocles is over the head of every member of the Liberal party who dares to take a stand that the government does not like.
This is pushing Parliament around. Sir, I know that skullduggery has been practised for years. This deed of endeavouring to force members of the House to vote for that which they do not want in order to get that which they do, makes a caricature of Parliament. This is legislation that constitutes a squalid subjugation of this institution. I have watched Parliament for a long while. I have a deep regard and affection for this institution. I saw parliament in the darkest days of war but, Sir, in the last two or three years it has been downgraded and degraded for one purpose only, as the hon. member for Pembina said when speaking on this matter, and that is to control the thought of Parliament because the government has a
March 31, 1971

Government Organization Act, 1970
majority. It is placing shackles, bridles and letters on this House. It is a dangerous bill.
The Prime Minister does not stay in this House when introducing his own bill. Even his parliamentary secretary is not here. On a bill of such importance, to which the Prime Minister placed his own name, it is difficult to understand why he is not here.
The explanation for what is being done is that it will provide flexibility and efficiency. This causes me to quote the words of Voltaire, who was referred to by the Prime Minister the other day, and who said, "There are some men who use thought only to justify their wrong doings, and speak only to conceal their thoughts." That is what is happening here. The Prime Minister recently indicated that the statesman with whom he felt the greatest affinity was Machiavelli. I have in my hand a volume called "Machiavelli The Prince". The Minister of Justice is looking at the picture on it and he will see that it bears a striking physical affinity to his leader's appearance. In fact, if it were not for the identification and the fact that this is a picture of a death mask, frequent mistakes would be made by those who look at it.
When a political philosopher receives the approval of the Prime Minister, it is interesting to read some of the observations. This is a Penguin Classic book, and I am sure all hon. members will want to get it. At page 91 I find this:
The fact is that a man who wants to act virtuously in every way necessarily comes to grief among so many who are not virtuous. Therefore, if a prince wants to maintain his rule he must learn how not to be virtuous, and to make use of this or not according to need.
Then, I shall read this part:
-he should not deviate from what is good, if that is possible, but he should know how to do evil, if that is necessary.
Here is another quotation:
-a prudent ruler cannot, and should not, honour his word when it places him at a disadvantage and when the reasons for which he made his promise no longer exist-a prince will never lack good excuses to colour his bad faith. One could give innumerable modem instances of this, showing how many pacts and promises have been made null and void by the bad faith of princes:-one must know how to colour one's actions-Men are so simple, and so much creatures of circumstances, that the deceiver will always find someone ready to be deceived.
The cabinet deserves to be mentioned and Machiavelli says:
-a shrewd prince should adopt a middle way, choosing wise men for his government-
Apparently, the Prime Minister did not follow that principle.
*-allowing only those the freedom to speak the truth to him, and then only concerning matters on which he asks their opinion, and nothing else.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
There are many other good statements here which indicate a dangerous philosophy. Here is another:
How princes should honour their word-praiseworthy it is for a prince to honour his word and to be straightforward rather than crafty in his dealings; nonetheless contemporary experience shows that princes who have achieved great things have been those who have given their word lightly, who have known how to trick men with their cunning, and who, in the end, have overcome those abiding by honest principles.

I suggest that the hon. member should remain seated, even though that gives him concussion of the brain. I suggest that he sit where he now is.
Clause 14 reads:
Where it appears to the Governor in Council that the requirements for formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters coming within the responsibility of the Government of Canada warrant the establishment for the time being of a special portion of the public service of Canada presided over by a Minister charged with responsibility for the formulation and development of such policies, the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a Ministry of State for that purpose.
I underline the words "developing new and comprehensive policies". This clause gives to the cabinet the power to set up what are, to all intents and purposes under this proposed legislation, temporary departments. Clause 15 reads:
A proclamation establishing a Ministry of State shall
(a)	state the name of the Ministry;
(b)	specify the matter or matters in relation to which the Minister for the Ministry is to formulate and develop policies; and
(c)	specify the powers, duties and functions to be assigned to the Minister for the Ministry in relation to the formulation and development of those policies.
I draw the attention of the committee to these words in subclause (c), "specify the powers, duties and functions to be assigned to the Minister". I also draw the committee's attention to clause 21, which reads:
In addition to the powers, duties and functions specified in the proclamation establishing a Ministry of State, the powers, duties and functions of the Minister for that Ministry extend to and include such other matters as are assigned or transferred to the Minister or the Ministry by or pursuant to any Act of the Parliament of Canada.
That clause provides that the cabinet has power to determine the powers, duties and functions of a department which is to be established as a ministry of state. It has the authority to extend those powers and give additional areas of jurisdiction to a minister of state. It has the power to end such a department at any time, without reference to Parliament and without any reference to any statute on the statute books of Canada.
When the Canadian Labour Congress appeared before the government to present its annual brief a few weeks ago, the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing suggested to the delegation that the whole question of housing could be speeded up if Parliament passed Bill C-207, so that a ministry of state could be established for housing and urban affairs. I am not in a position to know whether the Prime Minister intends to establish a ministry of state for housing and urban affairs although, certainly, the statement of the Minister without Portfolio to
the CLC delegation gives one reason to believe that that is the government's intention.
What does that mean, Mr. Chairman? Is a ministry of state dealing with housing and urban affairs within the terms of reference of the words of clause 14 that I shall now quote:
-developing new and comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters coming within the responsibility of the Government of Canada-
Does this mean that the government is now asking Parliament for the authority to set up, by order in council and by proclamation, a department of housing and urban affairs, without any reference to Parliament and without giving Parliament the opportunity to discuss the duties to be allocated to the minister, the powers given to the ministry of state and the jurisdiction which the minister of state will have?
A ministry of housing and urban affairs is not a temporary measure dealing with new and comprehensive policies. It is the kind of department that ought to be permanent. It is a department that will probably function as long as there are problems in housing and problems relating to urban affairs. Yet here the government is asking for authority, without referring to Parliament and merely by proclamation, to set up such a department, to extend the powers of that department and, when it deems it advisable, to end that department. Parliament is not to have any opportunity whatsoever to discuss the matter. Mr. Chairman, this is an amazing attitude for the government to take.

speechtext: It is scandalous.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
It is nothing short of scandalous that the government should ask for the power to set up departments of government without referring to the Parliament of Canada and to the elected representatives of the people the matter of what areas of jurisdiction should be available to such a department, what powers it should exercise and what duties shall be prescribed for the minister in question. Actually, this government has been consistently endeavouring to erode the powers of parliament. Already the control of the purse strings has largely passed out of the hands of Parliament. Estimates go to committees. There is no opportunity in the House except for a vote. It is true that a member may specify a particular item on which he wants a vote taken, but there is no opportunity for discussion. The control of the purse strings is increasingly slipping out of the hands of the elected representatives.
We are now asked to go one step further and give the cabinet the stupendous power to set up departments of government with sweeping powers. We are asked to give the government that right without any recourse to Parliament whatsoever. The President of the Treasury Board says that this is necessary in order to have a flexible response. I say that this request for a flexible response is

March 31, 1971

merely a subterfuge for asking for extraordinary and unparliamentary powers.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext: The fact is that technocrats, and I certainly include the President of the Treasury Board in that class, tend to become autocrats. They have little or no appreciation or understanding of the parliamentary process in a democratic society. If giving these sweeping powers to the cabinet is going to make for greater efficiency, it is logical to argue that Parliament be sent home, then, the President of the Treasury Board and the other technocrats could run the whole government of Canada. I say to members opposite that this steady and continuous erosion of the powers of the elected representatives and ignoring the role of Parliament in our democratic system is something they will live to regret.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Many articles have been written in recent months pointing out that the Prime Minister of Canada is moving more and more toward a presidential system and that increasing powers are being vested in the hands of the Prime Minister. It is no longer a case of prima interpares. It is a case of one man seeking to exercise more and more power at the expense of Parliament.
It is significant that the Prime Minister, who is sponsoring this bill, is not even here. When I asked him a few weeks ago if he would undertake to be present when we were discussing these particular sections, he said he would be here. He is not here. He, alone, is in a position to say to Parliament why he wants these extraordinary powers, the use he intends to make of them, what ministers of state he intends to appoint and what particular functions will be given to these ministries of state. He ought to be able to tell us whether these ministries of state will deal with temporary problems or whether he intends to use the powers in this bill to set up virtually permanent departments, such as a ministry of housing and urban affairs. Housing and urban affairs is not a temporary matter. If the government sets up a ministry of housing and urban affairs, I serve notice that in my opinion it will be a complete violation of clause 14 in Part IV of this bill.
The fact that the Prime Minister completely ignores the committee of the whole, has taken no part in the debate and has not seen fit in any of the preceding stages to outline the reasons for seeking powers which have never been granted to any Prime Minister in the history of Canada, indicates a contempt for Parliament. That contempt has not only been indicated by his absence from this committee, but it has been indicated by a number of actions which he has taken. As a matter of fact, in any democratic country, not even the president has the authority to allocate powers and duties unless such action is based on statutes enacted by the elected representatives.
In the United States, a cabinet minister has to be ratified by congress. The department over which any cabinet minister presides is based on statutes passed by
Government Organization Act, 1970
congress. He exercises powers which have been approved and passed by congress.

No, I am not suggesting that we move to the presidential system. What I am saying to the President of the Treasury Board is that we are in great danger of getting the worst features of both. We are going to get the presidential system without the controls and power to exercise restraint which are available to te United States congress. We will have neither the benefits of the Parliamentary system nor the restricted measures and restraints of the United States Congress.
This legislation is being rammed through the House. Opposition protests are being ignored with respect to the matter of setting up ministries of state. In the main, the government members have remained silent. We have heard no protests from them.

I suppose many of them hope to be appointed ministers of state or parliamentary secretaries. This committee would do well to stop and think of the long-term repercussions which will evolve from the step we are now being asked to take. The government wants to have a flexible response. There is certainly a case to be made for being able to deal with certain matters and to have certain ministers allocated to deal with specific problems. The government has the power to appoint ministers without portfolio and to give them specific jobs to do.
We have been asking for a long time that a department of housing and urban affairs be established. The government can bring in legislation to set up such a department. This would enable the members of this House to discuss the role of such a department, the powers that would be given to it and the duties of the minister in charge of the department. That would be the proper way to do it. However, when the government asks for the power to set up a department of housing and urban affairs or any other department on its own initiative on the subterfuge that this is merely a temporary organization, the government is seeking in a round about way to bypass Parliament and to nullify the powers of Parliament.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
On this question, members in all parts of the House have a serious responsibility to look into the long-term effects of this measure and to speak out on them. As the powers of Parliament are curtailed and as the voice of the elected representatives is muzzled, so the democratic process suffers.
We might as well face the fact, Mr. Chairman, that there is a growing body of opinion among youth today that parliamentary democracy is irrelevant; that the parliamentary system has had its day. I do not believe that.

March 31, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 I believe that the parliamentary system is one of the best systems that has ever been evolved to enable free men and women to have a voice in governing themselves. But if its elected representatives are to have less and less power, if they are increasingly to become rubber stamps, if they are merely to be brought together to vote for or against non-confidence motions and to ram through estimates on the last prescribed day, then Parliament and its reputation will suffer and a great many of the rising generation will be looking to other methods of governing this country.
This provision is a retrograde step. It is something that the government does not need. If the government wants ministers to deal with specific problems, then it has the authority to appoint ministers without portfolio, if the government needs to set up additional departments, such as a department of housing and urban affairs, then Parliament will support the government. Indeed, I think all parties in the House have at different times urged the government to set up a department of housing and urban affairs. Certainly, the Mayors and Municipalities Association of Canada has been urging this for years.
The government does not have to take this action through the back door, and I should like to ask why it is using this method. Is it because the type of legislation that it has in mind is such that it thinks the House will object to it? Or is it going to be such a piece of window dressing that a ministry of state will be created with virtually no power to be more than a sort of study group to give the Canadian people the impression something is being done when, in fact, the government does not intend such a ministry to do anything at all? I hope that the President of the Treasury Board will tell this committee the reason the government is adopting this method. If the government does want to set up a department of housing and urban affairs, I ask the President of the Treasury Board why it does not bring in a bill to set up such a department.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are currently studying Part IV of the act respecting the organization of the
government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto.
According to Clause 14, the government proposes to establish ministries of state which would handle various matters.
When perusing the legislation, one starts wondering what these matters are and why should a ministry of state be established. Clause 14 provides that ministries of state will be created. We therefore have to find in the bill in which specific areas the government intends acting in order to justify the creation of a department or a ministry and the appointment of a minister of state.
The answer to this basic question does not appear in the bill, nor is it mentioned in the government's statements, or those of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), because, at any rate, even if he is the sponsor of the bill he does not dare pilot it himself.
It is therefore nearly impossible for the opposition to find out why the government wants to create these new ministries of state. We must be satisfied with what is written, trying to justify honestly the establishment of these ministries.
Therefore, I would like to make a detailed study of some clauses of this bill. The questions I ask myself and that I want to ask my hon. colleagues are as follows: What definite fields will be covered by the ministries of state? Who will create them? And finally, whose authority will these ministries of state come under? Who will they be under? The government or parliament?
Therefore, I would like to study immediately clause 14 which states:
p.ra.)
Where it appears to the Governor in Council that the requirements for formulating and developing new and comprehensive policies in relation to any matter or matters coming within the responsibility of the Government of Canada warrant the establishment for the time being of a special portion of the public sevice of Canada presided over by a Minister . . .
This is the reason why the government wants to create a ministry of state. For some reason or other the governor in council will create a ministry of state in order to deal with a problem or to make some study.
Mr. Chairman, this reason means nothing, of course. It is simply a legal jumble which justifies nothing, explains nothing and does not say why a ministry of state will be created.
Mr. Chairman, I doubt then that we are justified in creating ministries of state. We are not opposed in principle and we expect it to be clearly understood. However, we would like to know what the duties of these ministries of state will be, why they will be set up and under what circumstances.
Let us assume for instance that a serious housing crisis exist all across Canada-such as the one now prevailing-and reflects unfavourably on the government in the public opinion. Let us assume that such a crisis is prejudicial to the government; let us assume that there is a very urgent need for a change in housing policy, that the

March 31, 1971

government is in danger of losing ground and of being brought to bay.
A similar situation could also prevail with respect to taxation.
The same could be said, for instance, of unemployment and of summer jobs for students, whom the government is unable to supply with summer jobs. It is merely applying poultices to wooden legs, palliatives which do not solve the real problem but seek to make people forget about it.
The government therefore, in order to mask its inefficiency and put people off, could announce, with a fine fanfare of publicity, of course well nourished by the mass media, the creation of a ministry of state headed by a minister without portfolio, to concentrate exclusively on the problem of summer jobs for students, or on student problems in general, or on housing, or on any other problem.
This does not mean that the problem would thus be solved. As a matter of fact, it simply means that to escape the storm, the government is using the ostrich policy, that is, it is hiding its head in the sand.
The government does not justify the establishment of this ministry of state, but in creating it, it tries to find a way to hide is incompetence, its apathy, its lethargy and its lack of action in a given field.
If hon. members on the treasury benches do not agree, I should like them to show me the provisions of the bill which assure them that such a ministry will not make unwarranted expenditures.
Of course the expenditure of public money is justified to the extent that we really want to face a special problem, and this with appropriate tools.
Mr. Chairman, today the government would have parliament grant a special power to the cabinet, that is appointing at will up to a maximum of five state ministers, and this for purposes and in circumstances which are not defined.
Mr. Chairman, having read the first part of clause 14, I must simply conclude that this is an ostrich policy. Moreover, as those who spoke before me said, this is a policy quite typical of the Trudeau government: the disintegration of the executive and legislative in order to crush the supreme institution likely to ensure the defence of Canadian people, that is parliament. This is a new way to cursh parliament, by granting the cabinet enlarged powers, without applying nor having to report to parliament.
I will go on with my quotation of clause 14 which stipulates that ministries of state will be established, for reasons that are not given, and that they will be headed by a minister of state.
The clause states, and I quote:
-charged with responsibility for the formulation and development of such policies, the Governor in Council may, by proclamation, establish a Ministry of State for that purpose.
Not only will parliament not be able to advise the government to establish a ministry or state nor to ask for its establishment, but the government will not even be
Government Organization Act, 1970 required to ask for the consent of parliament for this purpose.
Thefore, an extraordinary power is thus given to the executive, independently of the people's will and of their supreme protective agency, parliament.
Mr. Chairman, this kind of politics cannot be justified in any way unless we understand that we are considering the policies applied by this government over the last two years, which are unilateral policies showing utmost disregard for the wishes and requests of parliament and which, I must unfortunately admit, are initiated against the hon. members' wishes.
This shows how much this government mocks the House of Commons and reviles its power. It shows to what extent under the present government the executive attempts once more-and this time it is once too many- to crush the legislative power.
In Canada there are three separate powers which are all of equal importance: the judiciary, the legislative and the executive power. It is clearly understood that these powers can be exercised on the condition that the executive does not wield legislative and judiciary powers.
Mr. Chairman, all will recognize that from the moment the executive attempts to dictate some rules or guidelines to the judiciary, then justice is not justice anymore because it is directly dependent on the executive power. He who is judged cannot expect from justice that it be equitable; he can only hope to avoid the disfavour of the executive power which is ready to grind him. The judiciary system cannot operate normally if the executive power tries to control it.
The same applies to the relationship that must exist between te legislative and executive powers. If the executive attempts, one way or another, to assume or limit the rights of the legislative authority, or to ignore them, we come to the establishment of a dictatorship. It is a one-sided decision. The people, through their representatives, have no longer a voice in the administration of public affairs.
Those are the ones, Mr. Chairman, who will say to the people at the next election: "My dear friends, give us your opinion; the Liberal government has come up with a new way of asking the advice of the people, that is through white papers. Let us know your views, be really democrats, take part in the economic and political lives of your country at the decision-making level.
Mr. Chairman, this cannot be true. It is only bunkum, if the executive power crushes, as it is actually doing, the legislative power, that is parliament.
We cannot really live in a democratic country as Canada, Mr. Chairman, and thoroughly apply to the system unless the three main Canadian powers respect each other.
Mr. Chairman, I believe the legislative power is ready to respect the executive and judiciary powers and that the judiciary power is willing to respect the executive and legislative powers. But most unfortunately, one cannot honestly say that the executive power respects the legislative power.

March 31, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970
Mr. Chairman, not only is the creation of those ministries of state unjustified but to make matters worse, the duties of the ministers to be appointed at the head of those ministries are not clearly outlined. And in that respect I shall quote clause 21:
In addition to the powers, duties and functions specified in the proclamation establishing a Ministry of State, the powers, duties and functions of the Minister for that Ministry-
One should give great attention to this part because the duties of that minister will be defined here, and I quote:
-the powers, duties and functions of the Minister for that Ministry extend to and include such other matters as are assigned or transferred to the Minister or the Ministry by or pursuant to any Act of the Parliament of Canada.
Therefore, this means nothing. It is once more the same legal mess which is found in clause 14 of the same part of the legislation. In fact, the more you study this legislation, the less you can justify the setting up of these ministries of state. But, if you put yourself in the place of the government members, you have two reasons to support this bill: Either you do not believe anymore in the legislative power and you are willing to increase that of the executive or you intend, through this indirect means, to increase your salary.
Mr. Chairman, I am quite shocked that there are not more government members to state their opinions on this subject. These members have the same rights and the same privileges as all opposition members and I cannot quite explain to myself why the latter alone feel they have to take advantage of their privileges to defend the rights of Parliament.
Mr. Chairman, I should like to call the attention of the government members to that point. I should like to ask the minister who is piloting the bill in the absence of the Prime Minister, what is the reason for the establishment of these ministries and ministers of state. I should like him to tell us what he intends to do and to what extent Parliament stands protected under Part IV of the bill.
There are many ways in which Parliament can be protected. First of all, the discretionary power that the Prime Minister is seeking under this legislation, that is authority to appoint ministers of state without consultat-ing Parliament, should be curtailed. Nowhere in this bill can there be found a clause or phrase prescribing that the government shall consult Parliament concerning the establishment of some ministry of state or the appointment of some minister of state. Nowhere is it stated that the execuive shall consult Parliament or that the ministry of state shall have to report to Parliament.
It is rather curious to realize that under the law many Crown corporations and many departments have to make a yearly report to the government on the administration of public funds, and yet those ministries of state would be excluded.
The ministers of state would not even have to be responsible to Parliament. Were we to carry to extremes the implementation of that system, even the ministers of state could refuse to answer questions which members of the opposition could direct to them on certain matters relating to the administration of those ministries of state.
Once one starts to play with those powers, to crush the legislative power, to push it aside for the benefit of the executive power, one realizes that it is no longer possible for democracy to survive and the situation does not make sense any more.
Mr. Chairman, I strongly object to part TV of the legislation which the right hon. Prime Minister did not have the courage to come and defend in the House, although he is the mover. I am strongly against that part of the bill because it is unjustified and no reason is given for the expense of public money. Above all, it will not solve anything. Judging from their accomplishments, there are already too many departments and ministries of state.
What results can we observe? Someone is designated as Postmaster General and one year later he is dismissed. A year after a new Post Office Department is established in a sort of crazy game. In the meantime, people may be amused but the problems are certainly not solved.
If, at least, through part IV of the bill, the problem of existing destitution in the midst of abundance in Canada were solved, if at least the people of Canada were given the assurance that they could live secure and free, the bill would be useful.
Unfortunately, part IV does not deal with the commonwealth, the well-being of the individuals. Nowhere in part IV is the problem of unemployment, of welfare, of the young dealt with. There is only talk of appointing ministers of state. Why? To increase the salaries of government members in a disguised way, without having to answer to the people, in addition to giving the cabinet more power to crush parliament which has become the only institution really capable of protecting the people from this government which tramples them through its policies as well as the methods it uses.
Mr. Chairman, if at least, through part IV dealing with the setting up of ministries and the appointment of ministers of state, the people could be sure that they would be better protected, we could discuss the bill more easily.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not an easy task to participate in this debate. I say that because it is obvious from the refusal of members of the government, as evidenced now by the hon. member for York, to grant the normal courtesy that is given to members of this House to complete their statements. Obviously, even the government backbenchers are not interested in listening to intelligent debate on this bill. They go so far as to bar the right hon. member for Prince Albert and the Leader of the New Democratic Party from that courtesy. One wonders what is the use of participating at all. We seem to be talking to deaf ears. Perhaps the members of the government are not interested. Even if they are interested, it is obvious that they do not want to hear the legitimate views of those who might be opposed to some parts of the bill we are considering at the present time.
I say also, Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to participate in this debate when the Prime Minister, who obviously considered the bill important enough to sponsor it, does not appear in the House at any time when it is being debated. Indeed, we do not even see his parliamentary secretary on this occasion. So as a result we are, so to speak, talking to the wind. There is not very much hope that one could present an argument to which someone would listen, and in respect of which one would receive the type of encouragement which would indicate that perhaps an interesting consideration is taking place in respect of the contents of this bill.
Having said that, I share the concern expressed here this afternoon by those who have preceded me and those who have spoken at other times in this debate. In fact, I must say-and I have thoughtfully considered what might be an appropriate adjective here, so I do not use it lightly-that this is the most deceptive piece of legislation I have ever had to deal with in this House or that this government has ever presented because its real result will be far more sinister-yes, that is the word-so far as the parliamentary process is concerned than most of us in this House even realize or understand.
If the only aim of this legislation were to increase the number of ministers and parliamentary secretaries, that
Government Organization Act, 1970 might be one thing; but actually that is only one aspect of what this bill will do. In the few minutes I have at my disposal I shall attempt to show that it also erodes the very fibre of what this institution is. Considering the attitude of so many young people, and others not so young, toward this institution we should be asking ourselves every day what we are doing to strengthen this institution and not to weaken it? This should be the basic purpose, not only of those in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition but of those who support the government. I am concerned, and this is why I use such adjectives as "deceptive" and "sinister", because I see a further degrading and eroding of the place of Parliament in what I consider to be the most satisfactory way that man has devised to govern himself.
I want to point to just a few of the anomalies in the bill. It is not just a question that the government does not define what an enlarged cabinet will do, with particular reference to ministers of state. It is not just the question that the powers of Parliament are being eroded. There is also the question that the whole bureaucratic administration of government is being strengthened, is becoming more difficult to manage and, so far as the representatives of the people are concerned, is becoming more dangerous. I believe that Canada is the most over-governed country in the world. We have three levels of government, municipal, provincial and federal, and when we talk about government we have to consider all three levels. I know of no better way to emphasize this point than to say that if we were to add the total expenditures of all levels of government together, and then deduct from that total the various transfers that take place between those levels of government and compare those expenditures with the net national income of the Canadian people, that national income being what they earn through salaries, through dividends, through commissions, through the sale of their produce, and whatever other income they may have, we find that it costs Canadians approximately 47 cents out of every dollar they earn to govern themselves. That calculation is relevant here, Mr. Chairman, because this bill will increase the size of the bureaucratic aspect of government at the federal level.
Let us look briefly at the present situation. There are 155 government members in the House. The cabinet is made up of 29 members, including the Prime Minister and three ministers without portfolio. It is the largest cabinet we have ever had in Canada. There are 16 parliamentary secretaries. There is an assistant speaker; there is a whip and an assistant whip. There is a vice-president of the House committees, and there is the chairman of the committees. This makes a total of 62 members from the government side of the House who have specific jobs, other than just being elected members of Parliament.
If one considers the remarks of the Prime Minister when he upset the fruit basket of parliamentary secretaries last fall, at which time he indicated it was his policy

March 31, 1971
Government Organization Act, 1970 to rotate these lesser offices every two years, one finds that Bill C-207 will provide an opportunity for 139 of the 155 members on the government side to have jobs during any one Parliament. How will that come about? We presume there will be 29 cabinet ministers, just as now. Then, there will be ministers of state, and if you count them on the rotating basis that means five for one two-year period and five for another two-year period, making a total of ten. With 28 parliamentary secretaries for each two-year period, there will be a total of 56 over the life of a Parliament. There will be two assistant speakers over the life of a Parliament, two vice-presidents of committees of the House, two whips, two assistant whips, and 36 chairmen of committees. I repeat that during one term of office 139 government members will be able to hold office. This is something that is disturbing. All it can mean is a growth of the bureaucracy and an increase in the cost of government.
Let us look at the situation in a few other democratic countries. Britain, which has a population of 50 million, has 20 members in cabinet, and there are 30 ministers of state who are not in the cabinet. The latter cannot speak on policy. All they can do is answer for the activities of the departments with which they are associated. Then, there are law officers, an attorney general, two solicitors-general and an advocate making a total of four. There are 54 ministers, in and out of cabinet, out of a grand total of 630 Members of Parliament.

speechtext:
I have only 20 minutes, Mr. Chairman, and I have some material I would like to put on the record. Since there are no provincial governments in Britain, one must assume that the national government looks after much of the administration which is the responsibility of provincial and municipal governments in Canada.
Australia, with a population of less than 14 million and a federal system similar to Canada's, has 12 ministers hi the cabinet and 14 ministers who are not in the cabinet, for a total of 26. There are 21 ministers chosen from the Australian House of 125 members, and five from the Senate of 60 members, and that Senate is an elected body.
India, with a population of 500 million, has state legislatures like we have in Canada. It has a cabinet of 50 members. It also has 15 ministers of state who are not members of the cabinet. The lower House consists of 500 members. Then, there is the President of the Republic in addition to the Prime Minister, and he also has an administrative function.
The United States, with a population of 210 million, has 12 cabinet ministers, and they are not chosen from the House or the Senate. There are 50 state governments in that country.
France, with a population somewhat the same in numbers as the United Kingdom, has a cabinet of 19 members. Its National Assembly is composed of 779 members, and it has no provincial or state governments.
Germany, which is not too dissimilar in population from France and the United Kingdom, has a cabinet of 16 members. The federal parliament is composed of 496 members, and there are also provincial governments, the Landers.
Japan, with a population of 100 million or more, has a cabinet of 21 members, and its House of Representatives is made up of 467 members. It has no provincial governments. What I am concerned about is that the growth of bureaucracy, and the size of the government which has been pyramiding during the last three years, will continue.
In addition to the increase in the size of the administration, what concerns me also is the fact that under the terms of this bill the House will not be permitted to debate a proposal to form a new ministry. We all know what happened when Information Canada was set up without any reference to this House at all. I will have something to say about that in a minute or so. If we adopt this bill, we merely strengthen the power of the Prime Minister and the government to increase the bureaucracy without any reference to Parliament. By proclamation, the Governor in Council will be able to set up five ministries of state. In each case the responsible minister will be in charge of policy formulation and development. This is contrary to parliamentary procedure and tradition, since policy formulation has always been the prerogative of the Crown. This bill represents a real danger.
Furthermore, in clause 21 we find that the minister may be "assigned or transferred ... by or pursuant to any act of the Parliament of Canada". This gives the minister administrative powers besides his policy formulation duties. It is a way for the government to create another department without passing a bill, without the consent of the elected representatives of the people, without estimates and without study by a House committee. You can see what this means, Mr. Chairman.
The same criticism can be applied also to the actions of the Secretary of State who is responsible for bilingualism and biculturalism without any bill having been passed giving him this function. Perhaps we should recall that this was not just an accidental or single occasion. There has been a trend within the government towards such actions, and I believe that is the reason this bill has been worded and formulated as it has. By creating more ministries, the government is giving its ministers a licence to be absent from the House. The roster system governing the attendance of ministers has not worked so far. What will it be like with five more ministers?
The reasons for creating these ministries of state are obscure. The government already has the power to name ministers without portfolio. We have this situation in connection with the Post Office and Information Canada, with housing and urban affairs at the present time. Why create new ministries? For example, let us consider two

March 31, 1971

of the present ministers without portfolio, the minister responsible for housing and the minister responsible for Information Canada. They must be waiting in the wings to be established as ministers of state. I don't know, but if their jobs are so important that separate departments with a single minister in charge are necessary, whether that be a minister without portfolio or minister of state, then why not create full ministries? As has already been mentioned this afternoon, I believe the minister without portfolio in charge of urban affairs and housing holds one of the most vital positions in the government. So, why not make it a full ministry? I believe the majority of members in this House would agree with this. This could be done by statute and I believe there would be very little argument or disagreement about it. Perhaps the reason for not following this course is that ministers without portfolio now receive only $10,000 a year, while under the new statute ministers of state will receive $15,000 a year.
It is a well known fact that many of the Liberal backbenchers believe that they deserve a title. I do not really object to that because I know many of them are frustrated. They find it difficult to justify their presence in the House with the limitations imposed upon them. Indeed, they may be in a more difficult position than we in the opposition in many cases because there is not much opportunity for them to participate in debates as any member of this House should have the right to do. Rather than bringing a more logical approach to problems, the government is attempting to bring legislation in through the back door. It is a very deceptive type of legislation because it is in the form of an omnibus bill. Mr. Chairman, we cannot deal with the issues in the way we should under the omnibus approach to legislation. It is an unpopular method, and is only a tool to get legislation through Parliament without a proper decision on each item in the bill.
It seems to me that these points bring out some of the very real dangers that this bill represents. Another aspect worthy of mention is that there is no provision setting the length of time ministers of state can function. If we look at the various clauses of this bill, we find that clause 17 allows the Governor in Council to establish a ministry of state and a department, while clause 18 gives the Governor in Council power to terminate its existence.
Another deceptive clause is No. 20 which provides that a minister of state will not have a deputy minister but that his senior officer will be called a secretary, and he shall be chief executive officer. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, his function will be exactly the same as that of a deputy minister. If this is so, then why not give him the title? Soon there will be a deputy minister, under-secretaries and secretaries all doing the same jobs. Clause 22 provides that the minister of state will report annually to the House, but since there will be no Act to refer to it will be difficult to assess the report. It will be difficult to deal with estimates of such a ministry because there just will be no established committee to deal with them. Under the new rules, we are supposed to be giving all members a better chance to participate, but we are
Government Organization Act, 1970
already nullifying some rules to which we agreed not long ago.
We could talk about the uunlimited number of parliamentary secretaries that can be created. If we allow the government to do this, we are increasing the size of the bureaucracy and weakening the power of this House. At the same time we are increasing the power of the Prime Minister who already has more power than any head of state in any other democratic country in the world.

subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1970 PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEPARTMENTAL REORGANIZATION, MINISTRIES OF STATE, PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, my own leader, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, and the hon. member for Red Deer. They expressed in a very competent and serious manner the dangers inherent in this move to appoint ministers of state at the prerogative of the Governor in Council. All who are concerned and anxious about the welfare and good order of the parliamentary system will have enjoyed the remarks of these three hon. gentlemen, but I submit that they forgot something, Mr. Speaker. They forgot the very nature of the Liberal party-what the beast is like. In the history of our country there has never been another political party that has always known that it was the only one fitted to govern. There has never been a political party with a better reputation for lining up at the trough. It would be too much to expect the Liberals to have changed their ways during the life of one Parliament.

Yesterday the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way demanded a minister to look after the affairs of women. Hon. gentlemen opposite wili remember that up until very recently housing was cast from one department to another. I do not think there is one department that did not at one time or another have responsibility for CMHC or the National Housing Act. This may be one reason we have such a difficult time with housing in Canada at the present time.
I do not see that this bill is such a great threat. Indeed, the whole tenor of the speech made by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was that if the creation of these ministries was by separate bills in this House, then somehow the House of Commons would have some power. Probably since the day of Pitt the Younger, Parliament has not had any power except the power to delay. No hon. gentleman opposite can say that he really has the power to change anything, and none of us on this side can say it either. We have the institution of Parliament, of so-called responsible government, which sets the policies, and we can but follow. The opposition can oppose and delay. It is the delay that has discredited Parliament in the eyes of the Canadian people.

The parliamentary institution was well suited to a very quiet agricultural country. Canada is not the place for the old type of Parliament; we have to get things moving quickly and cannot be sedentary about policies. Therefore, between the idiosyncrasies of this Parliament which hon. gentlemen opposite so staunchly defend and the real facts of life in this country, we have to devise some new forms.
I think the Prime Minister himself when first elected as leader of the Liberal party said there was too much power in the administration. But it is no wonder when one minister has six or seven different departments to handle. An attempt is being made here to give one minister responsibility for a current issue, and the minister of the environment may not forever be involved with that particular issue. It may be the case that at the present time we do not even need a minister in charge of parks or in charge of lumber. After all, things change with time. I think this bill is an attempt to bring government to a current position. I do not say that it is perfectly right, but at least it is an attempt to recognize that if we make no changes whatsoever we will disappear. Not only will the power which Parliament may or may not have disappear, but our purpose in the minds of the people will disappear.
Unfortunately, democracy itself is put to the fore. When the people of Canada question our position, they also question democracy. The danger is that if we lower ourselves in the eyes of the people, what happens to democracy? I have tried very hard to follow the argument that has been put forward that the possible creation of more ministries will be so detrimental, but with all respect I cannot see it. I think this is a useful bill. It puts forward a set of criteria. It gives power to the government to create ministers of state for a certain specific purpose as the need arises, without going back for another 25 or 30 day debate. My right hon. friend from Prince Albert at one time held the highest elective ofiice in this country. He is a man who loves Parliament. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands was at one time premier of his province. Time was requested on their behalf for an additional period in which to complete their observations. This was refused. There is no doubt about where the denials came from. At least the hon. member for York-Simcoe identified himself when he challenged the right of one of our members to carry on. I think this was a shameful thing, and I regret it. However, it is not the issue we are debating today.
This is not the first time the government and its immediate predecessor have brought reorganization bills before the House. In 1966-67, Bill C-178 was introduced, a lengthy bill setting up a number of departments. In 196768 there was Bill C-161, and in 1969 there was Bill C-173. Each of those bills involved the reorganization of government, each of them reallocated responsibilities, established new departments and changed the functions of ministers. In addition, there exists at the present time an act which provides for the re-allocation of duties. Why is it necessary to proceed with the legislation we are examining today in this committee? What has been the net result of the three reorganization bills to which I have referred? They have resulted in the creation of a large number of new ministers who fall over each other's feet, get in the way, mess things up, and refuse to give hon. members information when they want it. Inflation is still with us, unemployment still rising, huge increases are noted in the cost of government. I should probably be out of order if I were to attempt to go into the details concerning the new departments which were created by the measures to which I have referred, and to the additional cost which has been laid on the shoulders of the taxpayers as a result.
Each time a new department has been created, spokesmen for the party opposite have said: we shall take over staff from an existing department, so it will cost less money; we shall set up these new, shining instruments and they will do the job so much better. What do we find today? The cost of government is abnormally high and is imposing a steadily increasing burden on the unfortunate taxpayer. Take the size of the Prime Minister's office and the Privy Council alone. In 1965, 125 people were employed in the offices of the Privy Council and of the Prime Minister. In 1969, there were 232. I believe the number today is around 300 or more. The cost of the Privy Council Office in 1965 was $2 million. In
1970 it was $11,256,175. My hon. friend from Churchill, during the debate on the budget on April 28, 1970, put some figures on record dealing with the establishment of the office of the Prime Minister, and I should like to quote now, from page 6223 of Hansard:
In 1960 the cost of the staff of former Prime Minister John Diefenbaker was approximately $50,000. The cost was the same when he assumed this office in 1957. One of the first things he did was to ask for the staff establishment of former Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent. The cost of Mr. St. Laurent's staff was $50,000. The cost of Mr. Pearson's staff ran in the neighbourhood of $75,000 until near the end of his regime when there were some sharp increases. However, this is a far cry from the $821,000 annually which is now being paid by the Prime Minister to staff his office.
That was in 1970, and there has been a substantial increase since that day. I understand that in the Prime Minister's office now there are some 80 people and that the cost is more than $400,000. This does not include the Privy Council staff. Maybe these people are needed, I do not know. But looking at the results, and judging from them, sure as Heaven something is radically wrong.
When the Prime Minister made his first speech in this House in this session, he asked that Hansard should record a list of the legislative programs referred to in the Speech from the Throne. There were approximately 70 measures proposed at that time, and since then the government has brought in two or three more. That speech was read three months after the conclusion of the last session. We were told by His Excellency, and the text of his speech was repeated by the Prime Minister in this House, that there were these 70 bills. This was the task facing Parliament. Surely, we had reason to expect that those bills would have been ready and would have been brought in for first reading right away. What did we find?

In other words, at the time the list of bills was placed on the record by the Prime Minister only eight were ready after three months of preparation and Heaven knows how much time before that. The only way to have an administratively competent and intelligent parliamentary government is to have a government which brings before the House a certain program, a government which states what the bills are and brings them in for first reading. In this way

the members and the people in the country may have a look at them. The opposition can then consider them, evaluate their position and decide what position they will take in the course of the session to deal with them competently.
Here, however, we find ourselves in the position that 30 bills have not yet been exhibited. I understand the situation is different in many other parliamentary governments. There is a time allocation, but not the time allocation this government thinks there is. This government does not know the difference between time allocation and the kind of parliamentary system we should have here. The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert referred to the difference between the presidential system and the parliamentary system. At least in the presidential system the president can appoint members of cabinet. This is precisely what the Prime Minister will now be able to do. However, in the United States every one of those appointments must be submitted to the Senate for advice and consent. The Prime Minister has mentioned that he would like to see a countervailing force. He has said it so often that some day I hope he will do something to bring it about.
It is necessary that government be strong. I have never denied the fact that under the circumstances of today, and the kind of society we have today, the government must be powerful and able to act quickly and efficiently. That cannot be down, however, unless this House is given the right to challenge, scrutinize and delay legislation if necessary. It is the parliamentary function of an opposition to delay if necessary and have a proper opportunity to see the legislation and deal intelligently with it. That is not a power which resides in this parliamentary system today. This government is now attempting to even weaken or limit what powers we have. Mr. Chairman, let no one say that the appointment of additional ministers of state or additional parliamentary secretaries will help the parliamentary system. In absolutely no way will this be the result. This is the reason we on this side of the House conceive it to be our duty to challenge the government on this issue.
My right hon. friend from Prince Albert and others have pointed out that this bill should not have been introduced in this fashion. There are aspects of this bill to which we might have given our approval in a minimum of time. But we would be derelict in our duty if we permitted this Prime Minister and this government to have this kind of power they wish to grasp. This is the name of the game for them. They want to have their hands on the levers of power so that they can manipulate things, not for the purposes of the country but for the purposes of the government and the party they represent. We would be derelict in our duty if we did not vigorously oppose this particular measure in this bill. The govem-

ment must have been aware of this. There was no hesitation so far as this party was concerned in disclosing to the government the fact that we intended to oppose this vigorously and at length. I consider, from the correspondence I have received and from the observations I have read in the media, that the government is on the wrong side on this particular issue.
I think the government would be well advised to review its position and withdraw this particular part of the bill as well as the next part. The government has the power it needs, so I ask why in Heaven's name the government is insisting on proceeding with this particular clause. I have indicated there is administrative incompetence and bungling on the part of the government. There is no question about this. Why do they believe the appointment of five new ministers will help? Mr. Chairman, I am glad to say a few words about the bill now under study. This bill is really bad when we consider all its wastefulness as well as the control it will give to some members of the administration.
Mr. Chairman, all parliament does is pass laws; it produces nothing. For the administration of taxpayers' property we now have hundreds of bodies which operate as best they can or nearly not at all.
We do not need new administrative tools, but more efficient ones. Should we fail to do that, it is futile to introduce other bills and complicate the situation even more by appointing new administrators with fantastic salaries which would contribute to raise government expenditures. All these new employees will not be able to do much more than today.
We provided ourselves with various tools: the Economic Council was established to give the government the tools required to have the economy operative. Several other commissions made suggestions to the government. They are there to advise the government on policy matters.
There are so many organizations which cost the taxpayers a mint of money, and still some people talk about setting up some more to solve the problem while the ones we now have are unable to ensure a better administration, because they are short of money. If we are to create new organizations and new ministries, more money will be required whereas there is still not enough of it for the ones now existing.
If we intend to increase taxes to enable these organizations to work properly, the Canadian taxpayers will no longer be able to pay because being already overtaxed they will go bankrupt and the majority of those who are now still thriving will eventually tumble down. The gov-
